item.title: Learning Chinese in vogue among Kyrgyzstan's youth
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-08
BISHKEK, Oct. 8 (Xinhua) -- Initially a fan of Chinese TV series, 19-year-old Zuura Zakirova is now a student of the Chinese language. Recently, the third-year Confucius Institute student at Kyrgyzstan's Osh State University performed a modern Chinese song and played the guzheng, a traditional Chinese zither, winning thunderous applause at an institute event -- one of her accomplishments after two years of Chinese learning. She loves watching Chinese fantasy TV series. "I am particularly fascinated by the actors' period costumes," a tiny part of her obsession with Chinese culture, according to her. Respecting the elders and valuing family ties, as highlighted by Chinese culture, particularly resonates with the Kyrgyz girl. "Our culture has similar concepts. I love it when my family gathers around the festive table and everyone chats happily. I feel happy in that warm atmosphere," she said. The experience of learning Chinese at the Confucius Institute has a profound impact on her, she said. "I've become more self-confident ... I was shy. Here, I've met many teachers and made a lot of friends." "Now, I can communicate freely with Chinese people in their own language," she said. Zakirova said she wants to be a teacher, just like her parents, and "I hope to teach the Chinese language to people in Kyrgyzstan and help with their personal growth through this language." As Kyrgyzstan's ties with China have deepened, learning Chinese has become increasingly popular among young people in the Central Asian country. The Confucius Institute where Zakirova studies has provided Chinese language courses for about 17,000 people since its establishment in 2013. Nearly 600 in total have won scholarships to study in China. Some graduates have returned to join the institute. Among them is Gulperi Kadyrbekova. One of the institute's first students, she became a teacher there in 2019. In her early days of teaching Chinese, what frustrated her most was the failure to immediately answer the students' questions about such broader topics as Chinese society or economy, she said. Hence, her extensive preparations for each class -- invaluable training and experience -- have brought her to career success today. Kadyrbekova takes pride in her students' successes, such as passing language examinations and earning overseas study opportunities. "This year, the first group of students I taught graduated from Chinese universities. Some have already found good jobs. I am so happy for them," she said. For Baikazak Sultanbekov, who studies at the foreign languages college of Jalal-Abad State University, the dream now is to get a chance as soon as possible to study in China. It was prompted by his cousin's account of living in China. "My older cousin studied at a university in Shanghai. He told me that Chinese is a difficult but interesting language, and that China is a rapidly developing country with skyscrapers and wide roads everywhere. Life there is very convenient," he said. "I felt envious, so I decided to start learning Chinese." The enthusiasm persists. "I think the most interesting thing about Chinese is its characters ... every Chinese character is like a work of art. That is precisely where their charm lies," he said. Vowing to improve his linguistic proficiency as quickly as possible, Sultanbekov dedicates nearly six hours of a day to studying Chinese. "In addition to my college studies and courses at the university's Confucius Institute, I review what I learned in class at home, read textbooks to prepare for Chinese language exams, and practice writing Chinese characters," the young man said, who also makes a point of speaking Chinese whenever possible. Sultanbekov plans to follow in the footsteps of his cousin to pursue further study in Shanghai, and to work in the future as an interpreter. "An increasing number of Chinese companies are operating in Kyrgyzstan ... This means I'll have a wide range of career options." ■

item.title: Three years into Gaza conflict -- destruction, deadlock and regional fallout
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-08
CAIRO, Oct. 7 (Xinhua) -- Three years after the Gaza conflict broke out on Oct. 7, 2023, the coastal enclave lies in ruins and tens of thousands have been killed. A ceasefire has been reached, but the fundamental deadlock remains unresolved. Analysts contend that irreconcilable differences between Palestinian and Israeli demands, coupled with the United States' perceived bias, have left a comprehensive end to the conflict and lasting peace out of reach. The was has also had far-reaching repercussions across the region, with instability spilling over into Lebanon, Syria, Iran and the Red Sea. GAZA IN RUINS, WEST BANK SQUEEZED On Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas's "Al-Aqsa Flood" assault saw thousands of rockets fired from Gaza and fighters infiltrating southern Israel, killing around 1,200 people and taking about 250 hostages. Israel then declared war and launched "Operation Iron Swords," pounding Gaza with airstrikes and a ground offensive that evolved into a prolonged and devastating conflict. Over the past three years, Gaza has suffered catastrophic destruction, leaving a profound humanitarian catastrophe across the territory. More than 74,000 people had been killed in the enclave since Oct. 7, 2023, according to Gaza health authorities. "Large-scale Israeli military campaign resulted in a significant number of casualties, particularly among women and children, widespread destruction of homes and infrastructure, and the displacement of more than two million Palestinians," Bahraini political analyst Abdullah Al Huwaihi commented. Amid mounting global outrage over the killings in Gaza, a ceasefire was eventually reached in October 2025. Under phase one of the U.S.-proposed Gaza ceasefire plan, Israeli forces were required to retreat to the "Yellow Line" and swap hostages for prisoners. Phase two, launched in mid-January, focused on the demilitarization of Gaza and the establishment of technocratic governance. By the end of July, Hamas had agreed to include the handover of heavy weapons in the demilitarization arrangements, conditional on Israel's full withdrawal and a halt to "aggressions." Yet the phased agreements have failed to translate into lasting peace. Khaled Al Hroub, professor of international conflicts at Northwestern University in Qatar, said the failure of successive frameworks shows that any real settlement requires moving beyond managing recurring violence to tackling the political roots of the conflict. Alongside the devastation in Gaza, violence and the erosion of Palestinian territory in the West Bank have also intensified. UN data shows that as of Aug. 10, some 3,800 Palestinians had been displaced by settler violence, house demolitions and evictions this year. The UN has recorded over 1,430 settler-related incidents this year, affecting about 260 Palestinian communities. "The West Bank is at the breaking point," Ramiz Alakbarov, the UN humanitarian coordinator for the occupied Palestinian territory, has said. DEADLOCK AND WASHINGTON'S DOUBLE BIND Analysts attribute the prolonged deadlock in Gaza to irreconcilable differences between Israel and Hamas. Akram Attaallah, a political analyst from Gaza, explained that Israel insists on Hamas's complete disarmament before any full withdrawal, while Hamas demands an end to Israeli military operations and a total Israeli retreat before discussing weapons. "Israel and Hamas view the issue as a completely zero-sum equation. Hamas wants to remain, while Israel wants to eliminate any presence of Hamas in the Gaza Strip," he said. "Between these two positions, the crisis continues." Baghdad University professor Adel al-Ghurairi said the U.S.-proposed framework, including the so-called "Board of Peace," the stabilization force and the transitional committee, remains largely on paper, with disarmament and Israeli withdrawal still pending. "The big pieces of the roadmap -- disarmament, an Israeli pullout, who governs during the transition -- are all still sitting unfinished," he said. Behind the scenes, the United States plays a deeply contradictory role, observers told Xinhua. Ali Al Hail, professor of political science at Qatar University, said Washington's role as chief mediator is undermined by its military aid and diplomatic backing for Israel, raising questions about its impartiality and allowing the conflict to persist. "The United States has played a dual role: it remains Israel's principal strategic ally while also being an essential actor in diplomatic efforts," he said. "This dual position creates questions about how effectively it can act as an intermediary acceptable to all sides." Al-Ghurairi added that the United States wants the war over, but it hasn't shown the will to actually force that outcome. "The absence of a genuine multilateral mechanism, and the reliance on unilateral American hegemony, renders any settlement fragile." SPILLOVER AND THE TWO-STATE SOLUTION Across the region, analysts see the conflict as having profoundly reshaped the geopolitical landscape. Sudanese political analyst Mohamed Amin noted that the conflict's regional spillover has been felt in the Red Sea, where Yemen's Houthis have attacked ships in what they describe as support for the Palestinians. "This has turned part of the repercussions of the Gaza war into an issue involving the security of international shipping and trade," he said. The balance of power between the U.S.-Israel alliance and the Iran-led resistance front, including Hamas, the Houthis and Lebanon's Hezbollah, has shifted, Al Huwaihi added. "Israel came to believe that, after what it viewed as its gains in Gaza, the confrontation should move toward Iran as the principal state supporting these groups," he said. "It subsequently succeeded in persuading the U.S. president to launch war against Iran on Feb. 28." Amid such complexity, the prevailing view is that true and lasting peace remains impossible without fully implementing the two-state solution and restoring legitimate Palestinian rights. Lebanese political analyst Youssef Diab said the Palestinian cause may remain a central conflict shaping the region. "There can either be peace for the Palestinians, including the establishment of a sovereign Palestinian state with genuine authority, or there will continue to be instability and chaos," he said. "Regional stability will also depend on the ability of regional and international powers to contain interconnected tensions in Iran, Yemen, the Red Sea, and the Gulf and establish broader security and political arrangements," Amin added.■

item.title: How 2026 Nobel laureates solve chemistry's "one-handed" mystery
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-08
STOCKHOLM, Oct. 7 (Xinhua) -- Hold up your two hands. They look almost identical and are mirror images of each other, yet no matter how you turn them, your left hand can never perfectly overlap your right. Many molecules behave in much the same way. This seemingly simple feature lies at the heart of the 2026 Nobel Prize in Chemistry, awarded Wednesday to French chemist Henri Kagan and Japanese chemist Kenso Soai "for the discovery of non-linear effects and autocatalysis in asymmetric organic synthesis." Their work helped answer a question that had puzzled chemists for more than a century: How can chemical reactions produce only one molecular "hand," as the chemistry of life does? WHY DO MOLECULES HAVE "LEFT" AND "RIGHT" HANDS? Some molecules can exist in two forms that have the same chemical composition but are mirror images of each other. Chemists call this property chirality, and the two forms enantiomers. "What makes chirality important is that life itself is selective about molecular handedness," Zou Xiaodong, a member of the Nobel Committee for Chemistry, told Xinhua. Amino acids, the building blocks of proteins, can exist in two mirror-image forms, but only one of these forms is found in the proteins in our cells. The sugars in DNA also favor one form. Chemists call this "homochirality," literally meaning "same-handedness." The mystery dates back to the 19th century, when French scientist Louis Pasteur discovered that some molecules could exist as mirror images. Yet when chemists later tried to make such molecules in ordinary reactions, they generally obtained roughly equal amounts of both forms. HOW DID KAGAN AND SOAI HELP SOLVE THE MYSTERY? The challenge was to find a chemical way to favor one mirror image over the other. Kagan took a decisive step in 1986. Chemists had generally assumed that if a catalyst contained a certain proportion of one molecular "hand," the product would show roughly the same proportion. He showed that this relationship could be non-linear. A small imbalance in the catalyst could create a much larger imbalance in the product. In simple terms, chemistry could amplify a slight preference. Soai then went further. In the 1990s, he developed a reaction in which the product could help make more copies of itself, a process known as autocatalysis. In one experiment reported in 1995, a starting imbalance of just 2 percent grew to 87 percent. By 2003, Soai had demonstrated a reaction that could begin without a built-in chiral preference and still end up overwhelmingly dominated by one mirror image. A tiny difference appearing by chance could therefore reinforce itself again and again until one molecular "hand" took over almost completely. Put simply, Kagan showed how a small chiral preference could be amplified, while Soai showed how that advantage could reinforce itself through autocatalysis. The Nobel Committee described the Soai reaction as one of the most spectacular chemical experiments ever conducted. WHY DOES IT MATTER? The discoveries help explain how homochirality can emerge, but their importance goes far beyond a century-old scientific puzzle. Chirality is crucial in drug development because the human body itself is chiral. Two mirror-image versions of the same molecule can interact very differently with proteins and other biological targets. "Drug molecules need to match the chirality of the human body, just as a right hand does not fit properly into a left-hand glove," Zou said, adding that being able to favor one molecular form therefore allows chemists to make medicines more precisely and reduce unwanted effects. The same principle is important in the production of flavors, fragrances, agricultural chemicals and some advanced materials. Kagan's discovery of non-linear effects also gave chemists a new way to understand and optimize asymmetric reactions, while Soai demonstrated how an extremely small initial difference can be amplified through a self-reinforcing process. That, according to the Nobel Committee, is why Kagan and Soai "made chemistry choose a mirror image." ■

item.title: GDI advances global development, South-South cooperation, says Pakistani envoy
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-08
by Wang Lu, Ma Ruxuan GENEVA, Oct. 8 (Xinhua) -- The Global Development Initiative (GDI) has played a key role over the past five years in revitalizing the global development agenda and promoting South-South cooperation, a Pakistani envoy has said. The initiative was proposed at an important time, bringing development back to the mainstream global agenda, which is an important contribution, Tahir Andrabi, Pakistan's Permanent Representative to the United Nations Office at Geneva, said in an interview with Xinhua. Over the past five years, the GDI has implemented more than 1,800 "small and beautiful" projects in more than 120 countries, mobilizing over 23 billion U.S. dollars, he said. Andrabi stressed that the GDI complements the Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) while responding to the reality that the world still needs greater focus on development. The latest UN data show that only 36 percent of the Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) targets with available trend data are on track or making moderate progress, and 15 percent have even regressed below their 2015 baselines. "The world, particularly developing countries, is falling behind in meeting the needs of its people and the SDG targets. The GDI is an important initiative to fill these gaps," he said. On China-Pakistan cooperation, Andrabi perceived the GDI as an important platform for charting the future trajectory of development and economic cooperation between the two countries. "We believe that the GDI, together with the BRI and its flagship project CPEC (the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor) 2.0, will continue to further diversify avenues of development cooperation between Pakistan and China in the context of CPEC, and between China and the larger developing world in the context of the BRI," he said. Andrabi expressed hope for deepening cooperation in high-tech fields such as AI, quantum computing and robotics, citing the immense opportunities in these areas. "The GDI provides an opportunity to make these technologies available to developing countries, thereby harnessing the potential of these technologies to deliver direct benefits and generate employment," he said. Andrabi also mentioned the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization (WAICO) established in Shanghai this year with Pakistan among its founding members. "We hope that WAICO, together with the GDI and the efforts of the Chinese government, will promote complementarities and work together to bring modern technology benefits to developing countries," he said.■

item.title: Frankfurt Book Fair 2026 opens with strong Chinese presence
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-07
Visitors are seen at the Chinese joint exhibition booth of the Frankfurt Book Fair in Frankfurt, Germany, Oct. 7, 2026. The world's largest book fair opened Wednesday in Frankfurt, Germany, bringing together more than 4,000 publishing institutions from over 100 countries and regions. The Chinese joint exhibition booth covers 336 square meters and features more than 3,000 titles and over 4,600 copies of selected books. It combines book displays, rights negotiations, cultural exchanges and interactive experiences. (Xinhua/Du Zheyu) FRANKFURT, Oct. 7 (Xinhua) -- The world's largest book fair opened Wednesday in Frankfurt, Germany, bringing together more than 4,000 publishing institutions from over 100 countries and regions. Over 230,000 visitors are expected to attend the Frankfurt Book Fair, which runs until Sunday at Messe Frankfurt exhibition center. According to organizers, this year's fair emphasizes international crises and conflicts, the application and regulation of artificial intelligence (AI), rights trading, children's and young adult literature as well as audiobooks. A wide range of lectures, forums, performances, book signings and readings will also be held to promote exchanges within the publishing industry, while giving readers opportunities to interact directly with authors, publishers and media professionals. The Frankfurt Book Fair is also one of the most important international platforms for promoting Chinese publications and copyright exports. The Chinese joint exhibition booth covers 336 square meters and features more than 3,000 titles and over 4,600 copies of selected books. It combines book displays, rights negotiations, cultural exchanges and interactive experiences. During the fair, Chinese publishing and cultural institutions will organize 55 events, including thematic seminars, dialogues with authors, copyright signing ceremonies and new book launches. Founded in 1949, the Frankfurt Book Fair has been one of the world's largest publishing industry events. ■ A reader is seen at the Chinese joint exhibition booth of the Frankfurt Book Fair in Frankfurt, Germany, Oct. 7, 2026. item.title: Changchun 2027 Winter Universiade unveils medals, torch
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-07
Staff members display uniforms and equipment at the 100-day countdown event for the Changchun 2027 Winter Universiade in Changchun, northeast China's Jilin Province, Oct. 7, 2026. The medals, torch, uniforms and equipment for the Changchun 2027 Winter Universiade were unveiled on Wednesday at a 100-day countdown event held at the Changchun International Aviation Expo City. (Xinhua/Xu Chang) CHANGCHUN, Oct. 7 (Xinhua) -- Medals, the torch, uniforms and equipment for the Changchun 2027 Winter Universiade were unveiled Wednesday at a 100-day countdown event at Changchun International Aviation Expo City. The torch, named "Ji Xiang," or "Auspicious Flight," is inspired by the clivia, Changchun's city flower. Its upper section features a filmstrip motif and 12 winter sports icons representing the Games' disciplines, a reference to Changchun's film industry. Snowflake and ginseng flower motifs appear near the top, while ski-inspired lines run down the sides and a wheel-hub pattern decorates the base. The torch stands 711 millimeters tall, a reference to the highest elevation in Changchun's urban area, 711 meters. The medals, named "Ji Meng," or "Auspicious Dream," combine traditional Chinese cultural elements, winter sports imagery and features associated with Changchun. The front features patterns inspired by skate blades and ski tracks, while the reverse depicts the "First Jade Bird of Ancient China," an artifact unearthed at the Wutaishan historic site in Nong'an, Changchun. Part of the bird design is inlaid with Songhua stone from Jilin. A filmstrip pattern along the medal's edge also references Changchun's film heritage. An embedded NFC chip allows athletes to access images of their medal ceremonies and seasonal scenery from Changchun by tapping the medal with a smartphone. Uniforms for torchbearers, torch escorts, volunteers, staff, technical delegates and ceremony personnel were also unveiled. The Changchun 2027 Winter Universiade will be held from January 15 to 25, with competitions in Changchun and nearby Jilin City. ■ The torch is unveiled at the 100-day countdown event for the Changchun 2027 Winter Universiade in Changchun, northeast China's Jilin Province, Oct. 7, 2026. item.title: China's railways see holiday return peak amid vibrant tourism market
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-07
Passengers are seen at the waiting hall of Tianjin Railway Station in north China's Tianjin, Oct. 7, 2026. As the National Day holiday is drawing to a close, return travel flows increase across the country. (Photo by Du Penghui/Xinhua) BEIJING, Oct. 7 (Xinhua) -- China's railways saw the peak of the holiday return rush on Wednesday, with 24.15 million passenger trips expected on the final day of the National Day holiday, amid strong travel demand and vibrant tourism activity across the country. A total of 2,449 additional passenger trains were scheduled on Wednesday to cope with the surge in demand, according to China State Railway Group Co., Ltd. On Tuesday, the country's railways handled 21.6 million passenger trips, marking the third consecutive day with more than 20 million journeys. Beijing, Guangzhou, Chengdu, Xi'an, Wuhan, Hangzhou, Chongqing and Shanghai were among the busiest cities for departures and arrivals, while passenger flows were particularly heavy on routes including Beijing-Shanghai, Wuhan-Shanghai, Wuhan-Shenzhen and Xi'an-Chengdu. Railway authorities across the country added services and expanded overnight operations to facilitate the return rush as China's tourism market remained vibrant during the seven-day holiday, with county-level destinations and nighttime consumption emerging as notable trends. County-level destinations gained popularity as travelers increasingly sought slower-paced and more immersive experiences away from major cities. From the coastal county of Lingshui in south China's Hainan Province to Mohe, a county-level city on the country's northern frontier, smaller destinations are drawing visitors with distinctive local experiences. Meanwhile, nighttime consumption flourished in many cities, with cultural performances, night markets, light shows and food fairs extending visitor stays and enriching holiday experiences. ■ Passengers are seen at the waiting hall of Shanghai Hongqiao Railway Station in east China's Shanghai, Oct. 7, 2026. item.title: Small counties, big appeal: China's "golden week" fuels diverse getaways
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-07
*During this National Day holiday from Oct. 1 to 7, authorities had projected 2.13 billion cross-regional passenger trips, averaging 300 million a day. *Cultural and tourism authorities nationwide have introduced a range of creative initiatives to attract visitors, drawing on sports events, cultural IPs, ethnic traditions and distinctive natural landscapes. *On Sept. 24, the Ministry of Culture and Tourism announced plans to develop more travel experiences that combine traditional culture with modern life during 2026-2030, aimed at helping foreign visitors travel more conveniently, enjoy more comfortable stays and gain a closer view of contemporary China. BEIJING, Oct. 7 (Xinhua) -- While tourism in China has traditionally been associated with breathtaking landscapes and photo opportunities, Wang Xin (pseudonym) opted for a different kind of National Day holiday this year: watching tennis. Well before the vacation she had purchased tickets for the Jingshan Tennis Open in central China's Hubei Province. A resident of Dongguan in Guangdong Province, about 1,000 kilometers away, she first learned about Jingshan because of the tournament. "I want to watch matches featuring several young WTA (Women's Tennis Association) and ATP (Association of Tennis Professionals) players up close," said the tennis enthusiast. She planned to spend three days watching the matches and the remaining four days exploring the county-level city, taking in its scenic mountains, valleys, and forests. During this National Day holiday from Oct. 1 to 7, one of China's few annual "golden weeks," authorities had projected 2.13 billion cross-regional passenger trips, averaging 300 million a day. Data from Meituan, a major services platform, showed homestay bookings for four-to-six-night stays during the holiday rose 24 percent year on year as of Sept. 28, with county-level destinations posting particularly strong growth. Cultural and tourism authorities nationwide have introduced a range of creative initiatives to attract visitors, drawing on sports events, cultural IPs, ethnic traditions and distinctive natural landscapes. DESTINATIONS FOR DIVERSE DEMANDS Jingshan, a county-level city where tennis has been developing for more than 40 years, is known as China's "hometown of tennis." To boost tourism during the National Day holiday, local authorities announced that during the tournament period, a match ticket would entitle holders to discounts at over 100 local businesses. Merchants have also benefited from the holiday travel surge. Zuo Meng, a vendor selling knitted products, said she follows the local tennis events closely. "In Jingshan, there are tennis matches almost every week," she said, adding that a tournament can generate 6,000 to 7,000 yuan (about 895 to 1,044 U.S. dollars) in sales. Over the past two years, she has also taught knitting skills to more than 200 women so they, too, could benefit from tourism. Peng Jufang runs a farm in Wenfeng Village. Noticing tourists' enthusiasm for tennis, he founded his own tennis club in October last year. With more than 16 people coming each day to try their hand at tennis, he was kept busy during this National Day holiday, teaching visitors for over six hours a day. In 2025, Jingshan hosted 48 domestic and international sports events. The comprehensive output value of its "tennis plus" economy surpassed 3.5 billion yuan, drawing 3.52 million visits for matches and tourism. While Wang Xin enjoys tennis matches in Jingshan, cultural enthusiasts have meccas of their own to visit. Wang Yinan, in her 20s, traveled from Beijing to Ruicheng County in north China's Shanxi Province after watching the popular animation "All Wishes Come True." Hometown of the legendary figure behind the film's main protagonist, Lyu Dongbin, Ruicheng is home to the Yongle Palace, which is known for its celebrated murals. "It is such an exciting trip, and it's incredible to be in Lyu's hometown," said Wang, as she browsed creative products at the Yongle Palace store. Liu Haibo, chairman of the Yongle Cultural Tourism Investment and Construction Co., Ltd., said the scenic site rolled out customized services to sustain its tourism growth following its viral popularity. Visitors can take photos in dedicated photo zones, guides explain the murals by linking them to scenes from the film, and tourists can attend interactive classes to learn mural copying and line drawing. The movie has helped raise the profile of Ruicheng, making it a sought-after destination, especially among young people. Statistics showed that between Oct. 1 and 5, Yongle Palace received about 80,000 visits, up more than 50 percent year on year. The ancient township of Fenghuang in Xiangxi Tujia and Miao Autonomous Prefecture, central China's Hunan Province, has kept its tourist momentum following the Sept. 25-27 Mid-Autumn Festival holiday. During the National Day holiday, some visitors seeking to avoid the crowds have ventured beyond the ancient town of Fenghuang into surrounding mountains and villages, exploring rich ethnic cultures, such as Miao welcoming rituals, lantern shows and folk performances. INTERNATIONAL VISITORS JOINING THE RUSH The diverse tourism resources in China's counties are also luring international visitors away from metropolises like Beijing and Shanghai and toward niche attractions. Lucas Martin, 28, from France, visited Fenghuang for the first time after touring major Chinese cities. "Fenghuang feels entirely different from big cities," he said. "You can slow down here. You can admire the distinctive stilt houses lining the Tuojiang River and observe local residents in their daily lives." The in-depth county exploration impressed him with the town's authentic living vibe. "This is not merely a tourist attraction. Walking along the river and pausing at street corners makes me feel more than just a passing sightseer." Emma Wilson, an Australian traveler who is exploring small towns and countryside across China, tried on Miao ceremonial costumes in Fenghuang. "It is magical to walk into the old streets, dressed like locals," she said. Shop staff carefully helped her get fitted in the ethnic costume. "A simple landscape photo fades quickly from memory. But putting on traditional clothing, tasting local food and learning the stories behind folk customs create experiences that stay with you far longer," she said. Since December 2023, when China launched a trial policy granting unilateral visa exemptions to visitors from six countries, it has expanded unilateral visa-free entry to travelers from 50 countries as of September, allowing eligible visitors to stay for up to 30 days. In a separate move, authorities extended the visa-free transit period for certain countries from 72 or 144 hours to 240 hours in December 2024. So far the number of eligible countries has increased to 57. Official data revealed that foreign nationals made nearly 61.29 million border crossings in the first eight months of 2026, up 19.5 percent year on year, while one of the leading mobile payment platforms, Weixin Pay, reported that both the value and number of e-wallet transactions made by overseas users rose by more than 80 percent during the same period. On Sept. 24, China's Ministry of Culture and Tourism announced plans to develop more travel experiences that combine traditional culture with modern life during 2026-2030, aimed at helping foreign visitors travel more conveniently, enjoy more comfortable stays and gain a closer view of contemporary China. FROM "CITY WALK" TO "COUNTRY WALK" Yang Han, a researcher at an institute affiliated to the travel platform Qunar, believes that county-level tourism began to accelerate around 2023-2024, as travelers increasingly sought destinations with fewer crowds, a lively atmosphere, opportunities for relaxation and immersive local experiences, as well as greater value for money. For instance, in Ruicheng of Shanxi, a set meal for one person may cost less than 20 yuan, the price of a cup of bubble tea in Beijing. Tuo Yanzheng, a professor at the College of Tourism and Service Management, Nankai University, said county areas hold rich agricultural, ecological and cultural resources with untapped consumption potential. "The key lies in turning these resource strengths into distinctive tourism products and consumption scenarios," she said. "It can not only meet people's increasingly diverse consumption demands, but also inject new vitality into the county economy." According to Sun Jiashan, a researcher at the Central Institute of Socialism, China's tourism market has evolved from "City Walk" to "Country Walk." Steadily improving transportation has made county-level destinations more accessible. By the end of 2025, China's total operating railway mileage had reached 165,000 km, including more than 50,000 km of high-speed rail. Shortly before the National Day holiday, the country opened four major high-speed railway sections, improving transport links across several regions and making travel easier for residents. The high-speed rail network is projected to hit 70,000 km by 2035, with eight north-south vertical lines and eight east-west horizontal lines. In addition, Sun noted that beyond scenic spots, historical sites and natural landscapes, tourists are increasingly drawn to vibrant scenes of everyday life, such as farmers' markets and bustling streets. "This shift also places higher demands on local cultural and tourism infrastructure and services," he said. "As overseas tourists venture beyond first-tier cities into central and western regions and county-level areas, they encounter not only the outward face of China's development but also the texture of everyday social life," he said. "This helps break through cognitive filters and information barriers in Western societies and presents a real China to the world." (Video reporters: Wang Xuetao, Yue Wenwan, Yan Rui, Hu Rong and Zhang Yujie; Video editors: Yang Zeyi, Zhang Mocheng, Zheng Xin)■
